h: Getting the most from the deer park
p: The deer are the stars here, and there are two kinds to look for. Fallow deer have roamed the park for centuries, and there is also a flock of Jacob sheep, a rare breed with spotty fleeces and impressive horns. The Lucy family are linked with bringing Jacob sheep to England in the 18th century, so they are part of the estate's story as much as its scenery.

The deer are wild animals, so admire them from a respectful distance. Autumn is the rutting season, when the stags bellow and clash antlers, and it makes a memorable sight, but give them plenty of room and keep children close. Quieter moments early or late in the day often bring the herd into view without much effort.

Inside, the house was given a big Victorian makeover in the 1800s, so you get a fascinating mix: Tudor bones on the outside, rich Victorian rooms within. Look at the Elizabethan gatehouse as you arrive, one of the oldest surviving parts of the estate, and see how the brickwork echoes the house behind it.

How long to allow? Half a day is comfortable for the park, gardens and outbuildings, longer if the house is open and you fancy lingering. It pairs nicely with Warwick, a few miles up the road, where Warwick Castle and the medieval Lord Leycester Hospital make for an easy second stop. Or head back into Stratford for an evening stroll along the river by the Royal Shakespeare Theatre.
